passage:
When my son's college friend Omkar came to stay a night with us in Ludhiana, I expected the usual: a boy who sleeps till noon and leaves wet towels. Instead he arrived with a small box of Kolhapuri chivda from his mother. After dinner he rolled up his sleeves and asked where the dishes went. I told him to sit; he dried them anyway. Next morning he made his bed, thanked my husband for the lift, and left before lunch, saying, 'Aunty, you must be tired, you cooked so much.' I was. I can't say what went on in his head, but I'd have that boy back any day.
Baljeet

qa.q: What did Omkar bring from his mother?
qa.a: A small box of Kolhapuri chivda.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel about Omkar's visit?
qa.a: Baljeet felt pleasantly surprised and grateful, touched that he noticed how tiring the cooking had been.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's actions made him a good guest?
qa.a: Bringing a small gift, drying the dishes, making his bed, thanking the hosts and leaving before they grew tired.

qa.q: Why might Omkar have chosen to leave before lunch?
qa.a: He likely sensed that hosting was tiring and wanted to leave while everyone still felt glad, though Baljeet can only guess his thoughts.

grounding: Shows a young adult guest who brings a small gift, helps in the kitchen and leaves before the host is tired, as seen by the host.

passage:
Friday: Before her trip to her college friend Tushar's home in Nashik, Farida, twenty-one, hunts for a gift she can afford and settles on a jar of her Nani's mango pickle.
Saturday: At Tushar's house she hands the jar to his Aai, then follows her into the kitchen. 'Let me cut the onions, at least.' Aai protests, then hands over the knife, laughing. After dinner Farida notices Aai's slow steps and says goodnight early instead of starting another round of cards.
Sunday: She leaves after breakfast, as planned. That evening Tushar forwards a voice note from Aai: 'Tell Farida she's welcome any time. Such a thoughtful girl.'

qa.q: What gift did Farida bring?
qa.a: A jar of her Nani's mango pickle.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she noticed Aai's slow steps?
qa.a: She felt considerate and a bit concerned, sensing Aai was tired and wanting to let her rest.

qa.q: Which of Farida's choices made her a good guest?
qa.a: A small gift, help in the kitchen, noticing tiredness and saying goodnight early, and leaving when planned.

qa.q: How did Aai experience Farida's visit?
qa.a: Aai felt respected and pleased, calling Farida thoughtful and welcoming her back any time.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult guest who brings a small gift, helps in the kitchen and leaves before the host is tired, showing that being a good guest is a skill.

passage:
Lavanya, before you go to your friend's house in Kochi, let your Manoj Mama tell you how I learned to be a guest.

At nineteen I went home with my hostel friend to his village for a weekend. I took nothing. I slept till nine, ate four times a day, and lay on their swing while his mother cooked for eight.

On Sunday I saw her sitting on the back step, rubbing her wrists. She looked so tired. I felt ashamed of myself.

So I washed every vessel in that kitchen, badly, while she laughed at me. And I caught the afternoon bus instead of the night one, so she could rest.

The next time I went, I took a box of Tirunelveli halwa and asked what I could chop. That family still calls me their second son.

A small gift, two hands in the kitchen, and leave before they're tired. That's all.

qa.q: What did Manoj take on his next visit?
qa.a: Manoj took a box of Tirunelveli halwa.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel seeing his friend's mother rubbing her wrists?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of himself for lying around while she cooked for eight.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Manoj visited?
qa.a: Seeing the tired mother on the back step; he washed the vessels and left early, and next time brought a gift and offered to chop.

qa.q: How might the friend's mother have felt when Manoj washed the vessels?
qa.a: She was amused and probably touched, laughing at his clumsy washing while getting some rest.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to be a good guest: bringing a small gift, helping in the kitchen, and leaving before the host is tired.

passage:
Disha had exactly four hundred rupees until the scholarship came, and Manjula Aunty had invited her for Sunday lunch in Chennai.

She couldn't buy a fancy sweets box. So on Saturday night, in the hostel pantry, she roasted besan and made a small jar of laddoos, slightly lopsided.

Aunty opened the door in a crumpled nurse's uniform. "Night shift," she yawned. "Come, come."

Disha put the jar in her hands and followed her into the kitchen. "What can I cut?" She chopped beans, stirred the rasam and laid the plates while Aunty sat down for once.

After lunch, Aunty's eyes kept closing mid-sentence. Disha stood up at three. "You sleep, Aunty. I'll come again soon."

At the door, Aunty held the lopsided jar to her chest. "These are better than shop ones."

qa.q: How much money did Disha have until the scholarship came?
qa.a: Disha had exactly four hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why did Disha stand up to leave at three?
qa.a: Disha felt caring and a little concerned; Aunty's eyes kept closing after the night shift, so she left to let her sleep.

qa.q: Which parts of Disha's visit made her a good guest?
qa.a: A small homemade gift, helping in the kitchen so Aunty could sit, and leaving before Aunty grew more tired.

qa.q: How does Manjula Aunty feel about the lopsided jar?
qa.a: Aunty is touched and grateful, holding it to her chest and saying the laddoos are better than shop ones.

grounding: Shows a young adult on a tight budget being a good guest with a homemade gift, help in the kitchen and an early goodbye.

passage:
For Christmas lunch, Elizabeth's family filled their Frazer Town flat with twenty-two people, and Pema was the only one who wasn't related.

She had brought a small packet of tea from her mother's garden in Sikkim, wrapped in newspaper and red ribbon. Elizabeth's grandmother sniffed it and smiled.

When the plates were cleared, Pema slipped into the kitchen and started drying dishes next to Elizabeth's aunt. "Guests don't wash!" the aunt protested. "I'm only drying," Pema said, and kept going.

At five she noticed the grandmother nodding in her chair and Elizabeth's mother leaning on the counter. Pema found her bag. "Thank you for having me. It was the best Christmas lunch I've had away from home."

Elizabeth walked her to the gate. "Amma says you're welcome any time. She never says that."

qa.q: What did Pema bring?
qa.a: Pema brought a small packet of tea from her mother's garden in Sikkim.

qa.q: Why did Pema decide to leave at five?
qa.a: Pema felt concerned for her hosts, noticing the grandmother nodding and Elizabeth's mother tired, and didn't want to overstay.

qa.q: What small things made Pema a welcome guest?
qa.a: A modest personal gift, quietly drying dishes, and leaving with thanks before her hosts were worn out.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth's mother see Pema?
qa.a: She clearly liked her, saying Pema is welcome any time, which Elizabeth says she never says.

grounding: Shows a young adult visiting well: a small gift, help in the kitchen, and leaving before the hosts are tired.

passage:
"Sachin, what's in the box?"
"Just some sweets for your mother, Mohit. From the shop near my hostel."
"You didn't have to."
"My Nani would kill me if I came empty-handed."
Mohit's mother opened the door. "Arre, Sachin! Come, come."
"Namaste, aunty. These are for you."
After lunch, Sachin stood up and began stacking plates.
"Beta, sit, you're a guest!"
"Please, aunty, let me at least carry them to the kitchen."
She laughed and let him. In the kitchen he dried the dishes while she washed.
At four, Mohit's father yawned for the third time.
Sachin picked up his bag. "Uncle, aunty, thank you. That was the best rajma I've had since I left home."
"Stay for tea!"
"Next time, aunty. You've already fed me like a king."
At the gate, Mohit said, "My mother's going to compare every friend to you now."

qa.q: What did Sachin bring for Mohit's mother?
qa.a: Sweets from the shop near Sachin's hostel.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Mohit's father yawned for the third time?
qa.a: Sachin probably felt thoughtful and a little concerned, sensing the hosts were tired and it was time to leave.

qa.q: What made Sachin a good guest?
qa.a: He brought a small gift, helped in the kitchen, thanked his hosts warmly and left before they were too tired.

qa.q: How does Mohit's mother see Sachin?
qa.a: She sees him as a warm, well-mannered guest, so much that Mohit thinks she will compare every friend to him.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who brings a small gift, helps in the kitchen and leaves before the hosts are tired.
